sidebar.keyIdeasHint: Keep these ideas beside the activity.

page1.idea1: Training starts with text that already exists.
page1.idea2: The model predicts before the real next Token is revealed.
page1.idea3: The training text supplies the real target Token.
page1.idea4: Prediction and target can be compared.

page2.idea1: A mismatch creates a correction signal.
page2.idea3: Training nudges many numbers by tiny amounts.
page2.idea4: One example changes the model only a little.

page3.idea1: The same loop runs across many text examples.
page3.idea2: Every example supplies its own known target.
page3.idea4: Training is not just storing complete sentences.

page4.idea1: Training happens before the model is used.
page4.idea4: Training and generation are different loops.

page1.title: Where do prediction probabilities come from?
page1.subtitle: See how training compares a prediction with the real next Token in existing text.
page1.lesson4: Lesson 4: Use learned patterns to predict
page1.lesson5: Lesson 5: Learn where those patterns came from
page1.intro: The model predicts before the training text reveals what actually came next.
page1.targetCovered: The answer is already in the text, but hidden for now.
page1.targetKnown: Known target from the training text
page1.technical: A training example is a piece of existing text with a real next Token the training system can use as a target.
page1.takeaway: Training can compare a model prediction with the next Token that really appeared in existing text.

page2.title: How does the model improve a prediction?
page2.subtitle: A correction signal nudges many adjustable numbers by tiny amounts.
page2.manyNumbers: These controls stand for many adjustable numbers working together—not one slot for each word.
page2.oneExample: The target Token becomes more likely for this example, one small step at a time.
page2.technical: A parameter is one of the many adjustable numbers inside a model. During training, many parameters are changed by tiny amounts.
page2.weight: Loss measures the prediction gap. A gradient tells the optimiser which small parameter changes would reduce it.
page2.takeaway: Compare with the real target, measure the gap, adjust many parameters a little, then repeat across many examples.

page3.title: Why does training use so many examples?
page3.subtitle: Watch the predict, reveal, compare and adjust loop repeat across existing text.
page3.allProcessed: All four examples passed through the loop.
page3.technical: Generalisation means learned numerical patterns can help with new combinations of text. Training is not simply a database of complete sentences.
page3.takeaway: One example changes the model only a little. Repeating the loop across huge amounts of text gradually shapes useful prediction patterns.

page4.title: Training vs Generation
page4.subtitle: Connect how prediction patterns are learned with how they are later used.
page4.bridge: Training changes these parameters. Generation later uses them to predict new text.
page4.point1: Training uses real text with known next Tokens.
page4.point2: Prediction errors guide tiny changes to many parameters.
page4.point3: Repeating this across many examples creates patterns used during generation.
page4.technical: Learned parameters are the adjustable numbers after training. During generation, the model uses their combined patterns; it does not look up a stored sentence answer.
